items.title_en: What "agent" actually means: a loop of LLM plus tools plus memory
items.title_zh: "Agent"实际意味着什么: LLM 加工具加记忆的循环
items.body_en:
**Definition**

An agent is an LLM that runs in a loop, deciding what to do next based on the results of previous steps, with access to tools and some form of memory. The defining feature is the loop. A single LLM call is not an agent. An LLM that calls a tool once is not an agent. An LLM that keeps going until a task is done, choosing its own next step, is an agent.

**Why it matters in delivery**

"Agent" is the most overloaded word in AI right now. Clients use it to mean anything from a chatbot to a fully autonomous worker. PMs who can ground the conversation in a precise definition save scoping nightmares. Agents also have fundamentally different cost, latency, and reliability profiles than single shot LLM calls, and getting this wrong destroys project economics.

**How it works**

The core loop:

```
[Goal or task]
    -> [LLM decides: which tool, which action, or done?]
    -> [Execute the action (call tool, run code, search)]
    -> [Observe the result]
    -> [Add result to context, loop back to LLM]
    ... continues until done or stopped ...
    -> [Final answer or action]
```

The components:

| Component | What it does | Example |
|---|---|---|
| LLM (the brain) | Decides next step at each loop iteration | Claude, GPT, Gemini |
| Tools | The actions the agent can take | Search, calculator, database query, send email |
| Memory | What the agent remembers across loop iterations | Conversation history, scratchpad, retrieved facts |
| Orchestration | The code that runs the loop and enforces limits | Custom code, LangGraph, OpenAI Agents SDK |
| Stop conditions | When the loop ends | Task done, max steps, error, timeout |

**PM decision points**

- Does the task actually require a loop, or would a single LLM call plus retrieval work?
- What is the max number of steps before the agent should stop and ask a human?
- How will we measure agent performance, completion rate is not enough, you also need quality and cost per task?

**Watch outs**

- Clients say "agent" when they mean "chatbot," always clarify what they really want
- Agents fail in compounding ways, each step has some error rate, multiply across steps
- The most reliable agentic systems are the ones with the fewest steps and the most constrained tools

**Takeaway: an agent is an LLM in a loop with tools. Use the word precisely or scope will spiral.**

**Qantas story**

Across Qantas, the word "agent" gets used to mean very different things in different conversations. A customer service chatbot is sometimes called an agent. A workflow that processes inbound emails through a fixed pipeline is sometimes called an agent. A genuine autonomous system that decides its own steps is also called an agent. Without a precise definition, scoping conversations go in circles.

Consider where a true agent earns its complexity at Qantas. Disruption recovery is a strong candidate. When a major operational event happens (a runway closure, a major aircraft technical issue, a crew shortage), the recovery decisions involve multiple data sources (flight schedules, crew rosters, aircraft positioning, customer manifests), multiple constraints (duty time, maintenance, slot rules), and multiple possible actions (cancel, delay, rebook, swap, divert). The order and combination of these decisions cannot be specified up front because each step depends on what the previous step revealed.

An agent designed for this would have access to a defined set of tools (read schedule, read crew roster, read aircraft availability, read customer manifest, simulate proposed changes, draft customer notifications). It would loop, deciding its next action based on what it has learned so far. It would stop when a recovery plan is fully defined and ready for human approval.

This is a genuinely agentic problem. The shape of the task cannot be pre specified. The agent does the thinking that a senior duty manager would otherwise do in their head. The cost per task is high (many model calls, large context, expensive flagship model) but the value per task is also high (a good recovery plan saves hundreds of thousands of dollars per major disruption).

Conversely, most Qantas use cases do not need agents. Customer service queries, content generation, knowledge search, structured data extraction, these are all single shot or short pipeline tasks that a basic LLM call with retrieval or tool use handles well. Wrapping them in an agent loop adds cost and unreliability for no benefit.

For AI delivery, the takeaway is that "let us build an agent" is rarely the right answer to an enterprise problem. The right question is whether the task genuinely requires a loop of decision making, or whether it is a single shot transformation that the team is fashionably overengineering. Agents earn their keep on tasks where the path cannot be pre specified. For everything else, simpler is better, and pretending a single shot pipeline is an agent does not make it one.
items.body_zh:
**定义**

Agent 是在循环中运行的 LLM,根据先前步骤的结果决定下一步做什么,可以访问工具和某种形式的记忆。定义特征是循环。单个 LLM 调用不是 agent。调用一次工具的 LLM 不是 agent。一直运行直到任务完成,选择自己下一步的 LLM,就是 agent。

**为何在交付中重要**

"Agent"是 AI 中最被过度使用的词。客户用它意味着从聊天机器人到完全自主的工作者的任何东西。能够将对话基于精确定义的 PM 节省了需求确定噩梦。Agent 还具有与单次 LLM 调用根本不同的成本、延迟和可靠性画像,把这弄错会破坏项目经济学。

**运作原理**

核心循环:

```
[目标或任务]
    -> [LLM 决定: 哪个工具,哪个行动,或完成?]
    -> [执行行动 (调用工具,运行代码,搜索)]
    -> [观察结果]
    -> [将结果添加到上下文,循环回到 LLM]
    ... 继续直到完成或停止 ...
    -> [最终答案或行动]
```

组件:

| 组件 | 它做什么 | 示例 |
|---|---|---|
| LLM (大脑) | 在每次循环迭代时决定下一步 | Claude、GPT、Gemini |
| 工具 | agent 可以采取的行动 | 搜索、计算器、数据库查询、发送电子邮件 |
| 记忆 | agent 在循环迭代中记住的内容 | 对话历史、便签簿、检索的事实 |
| 编排 | 运行循环并强制执行限制的代码 | 自定义代码、LangGraph、OpenAI Agents SDK |
| 停止条件 | 循环何时结束 | 任务完成、最大步骤、错误、超时 |

**PM 决策点**

- 任务是否真的需要循环,或者单一 LLM 调用加检索就够?
- agent 在停下来询问人类之前的最大步骤数是多少?
- 我们将如何衡量 agent 性能,完成率不够,你还需要每任务的质量和成本?

**注意事项**

- 客户说"agent"时意味着"聊天机器人",总是澄清他们真正想要什么
- Agent 以复合方式失败,每一步都有一些错误率,跨步骤相乘
- 最可靠的 agentic 系统是步骤最少和工具最受约束的

**要点总结: agent 是带工具的循环中的 LLM。精确使用这个词,否则范围会失控。**

**Qantas 案例**

在 Qantas 内部,"agent"这个词在不同对话中被用来表示非常不同的事物。客户服务聊天机器人有时被称为 agent。通过固定 pipeline 处理入站电子邮件的工作流有时被称为 agent。决定自己步骤的真正自主系统也被称为 agent。没有精确定义,需求确定对话陷入循环。

考虑真正 agent 在 Qantas 赢得其复杂性的地方。中断恢复是一个强候选。当重大运营事件发生时 (跑道关闭、重大飞机技术问题、机组短缺),恢复决策涉及多个数据源 (航班时刻表、机组排班、飞机定位、客户名单)、多个约束 (值勤时间、维护、时刻规则),以及多个可能的行动 (取消、延迟、重新预订、调换、改道)。这些决策的顺序和组合无法预先指定,因为每一步取决于前一步揭示了什么。

为此设计的 agent 将访问一组已定义的工具 (读取时刻表、读取机组名单、读取飞机可用性、读取客户名单、模拟拟议变更、起草客户通知)。它将循环,根据迄今为止学到的内容决定下一个行动。当恢复计划完全定义并准备好人工批准时,它将停止。

这是一个真正的 agentic 问题。任务的形状无法预先指定。Agent 做高级值班经理本来会在头脑中做的思考。每任务的成本很高 (许多模型调用、大上下文、昂贵的旗舰模型),但每任务的价值也很高 (一个好的恢复计划在每次重大中断中节省数十万美元)。

相反,大多数 Qantas 用例不需要 agents。客户服务查询、内容生成、知识搜索、结构化数据提取,这些都是单次或短 pipeline 任务,基本 LLM 调用加检索或工具使用很好地处理。将它们包装在 agent 循环中增加成本和不可靠性,而无好处。

对 AI 交付来说,要点是"让我们构建一个 agent"很少是企业问题的正确答案。正确的问题是任务是否真正需要决策循环,或者它是团队时髦地过度工程化的单次转换。Agents 在路径无法预先指定的任务上赢得它们的费用。对于其他一切,更简单更好,假装单次 pipeline 是 agent 并不会使它成为一个。

items.title_en: Tool use and function calling, the building block of everything agentic
items.title_zh: 工具使用和 function calling,一切 agentic 的构建块
items.body_en:
**Definition**

Tool use (also called function calling) is the mechanism by which an LLM can request that an external function be executed, receive the result, and incorporate it into its response. The model does not run the tool itself, it generates a structured request that your code executes and returns. Tools can be anything: a search API, a calculator, a database query, a third party service.

**Why it matters in delivery**

Tool use is the bridge between language models and real systems. Without it, an LLM is a closed box that can only generate text. With it, the LLM can read your CRM, query your database, send emails, call third party APIs, and act in the world. Every agentic system, every modern chatbot that does anything useful, runs on tool use.

**How it works**

The four step pattern:

1. You describe tools to the model in its system prompt or via the API's tool parameter (name, what it does, what inputs it takes)
2. The model decides whether to call a tool, and which one, based on the user's message
3. Your code receives the tool call, executes it, returns the result
4. The model reads the result and either calls another tool or generates a final answer

A typical tool definition:

```
{
  "name": "search_customer",
  "description": "Look up a customer by email or phone number",
  "parameters": {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
      "email": {"type": "string"},
      "phone": {"type": "string"}
    }
  }
}
```

| Tool type | Example | Risk profile |
|---|---|---|
| Read only data lookup | Search products, get weather, query stock | Low, hard to do damage |
| Write operations | Update CRM, send email, create ticket | Medium, can affect real systems |
| Code execution | Run Python, run SQL | High, sandbox required |
| External API calls | Stripe, Slack, third party services | Variable, depends on auth and scope |
| Long running operations | File processing, batch jobs | Needs async handling |

**PM decision points**

- Which tools does the agent actually need on day one, fewer is almost always better
- Are write operations gated by human approval, or fully autonomous?
- What happens when a tool fails or returns an error, how does the model recover?

**Watch outs**

- Too many tools confuse the model, it picks the wrong one or hallucinates parameters
- Tool descriptions are part of the prompt, vague descriptions lead to misuse
- Tool authentication and authorisation is a real security surface, treat it like API security

**Takeaway: tool use turns LLMs from talkers into doers. Scope tools tightly, gate write operations, monitor everything.**

**Qantas story**

Tool use is where AI moves from interesting to genuinely useful at Qantas. Consider a hypothetical AI assistant for the Frequent Flyer team handling member inquiries. The assistant on its own can talk about points programs in general, but it cannot answer the questions that matter (what is my balance, can I upgrade this booking, am I eligible for status match). Those questions require reading from Qantas systems.

The tool set might include lookup member by email or membership number, get current points balance and status tier, check upgrade availability for a specific booking, calculate points required for a specific reward redemption, retrieve recent activity, and check eligibility for specific promotions. Each tool is a thin wrapper around an existing system or API, exposed to the model with a clear description and parameter schema.

The interesting design question is how to handle write operations. Should the AI be able to actually redeem points, change a booking, or apply a status match? The conservative answer at most large enterprises is no, every write operation goes through a human approval step. The AI prepares the action, presents it for review, and the human commits it. This trades automation for safety, and at Qantas brand standards, that trade is usually worth it.

The other interesting question is how many tools to expose. The temptation is to give the agent every tool that might be useful. The reality is that more tools confuse the model. With ten tools, the agent picks the right one most of the time. With fifty tools, the failure rate on tool selection grows noticeably. The discipline is to expose the minimum tool set for the use case and add tools deliberately as evals demonstrate value.

Tool design is also under appreciated. A poorly designed tool with vague parameter descriptions and inconsistent error responses confuses the model. A well designed tool with clear descriptions, strict parameter validation, and informative error messages helps the agent recover from mistakes. The tool layer is product design as much as engineering.

For AI delivery, the broader lesson is that tool use is where AI delivery work intersects with the rest of the enterprise tech stack. The model is just the brain. The tools are how it reaches into existing systems. Designing those tools well, with proper scoping, validation, observability, and human approval gates, is what turns a chatbot demo into a real production system. Teams that treat tool design as an afterthought ship demos. Teams that treat it as core engineering ship products.
items.body_zh:
**定义**

工具使用 (也称为 function calling) 是 LLM 可以请求执行外部函数、接收结果,并将其纳入响应的机制。模型本身不运行工具,它生成一个结构化请求,你的代码执行并返回。工具可以是任何东西: 搜索 API、计算器、数据库查询、第三方服务。

**为何在交付中重要**

工具使用是语言模型和真实系统之间的桥梁。没有它,LLM 是一个只能生成文本的封闭盒子。有了它,LLM 可以读取你的 CRM、查询你的数据库、发送电子邮件、调用第三方 API,并在世界中行动。每个 agentic 系统、每个做有用事情的现代聊天机器人,都运行在工具使用上。

**运作原理**

四步模式:

1. 你在其 system prompt 中或通过 API 的 tool 参数向模型描述工具 (名称、它做什么、它接受什么输入)
2. 模型根据用户消息决定是否调用工具,以及哪一个
3. 你的代码接收工具调用,执行它,返回结果
4. 模型读取结果并要么调用另一个工具,要么生成最终答案

典型的工具定义:

```
{
  "name": "search_customer",
  "description": "按电子邮件或电话号码查找客户",
  "parameters": {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
      "email": {"type": "string"},
      "phone": {"type": "string"}
    }
  }
}
```

| 工具类型 | 示例 | 风险画像 |
|---|---|---|
| 只读数据查询 | 搜索产品、获取天气、查询股票 | 低,难以造成损害 |
| 写操作 | 更新 CRM、发送电子邮件、创建工单 | 中,可能影响真实系统 |
| 代码执行 | 运行 Python、运行 SQL | 高,需要沙箱 |
| 外部 API 调用 | Stripe、Slack、第三方服务 | 可变,取决于认证和范围 |
| 长时间运行的操作 | 文件处理、批处理作业 | 需要异步处理 |

**PM 决策点**

- agent 在第一天实际需要哪些工具,更少几乎总是更好
- 写操作是否通过人工批准把关,或完全自主?
- 当工具失败或返回错误时会发生什么,模型如何恢复?

**注意事项**

- 太多工具会混淆模型,它选择错误的或幻觉参数
- 工具描述是 prompt 的一部分,模糊的描述导致误用
- 工具认证和授权是真实的安全表面,像 API 安全一样对待

**要点总结: 工具使用将 LLM 从说话者变成实干家。紧密地界定工具范围,把关写操作,监控一切。**

**Qantas 案例**

工具使用是 AI 在 Qantas 从有趣变得真正有用的地方。考虑一个为处理会员咨询的 Frequent Flyer 团队的假设 AI 助手。助手本身可以一般地谈论积分计划,但它不能回答重要的问题 (我的余额是多少、我可以升级这个预订吗、我有资格进行状态匹配吗)。这些问题需要从 Qantas 系统读取。

工具集可能包括按电子邮件或会员号查找会员、获取当前积分余额和状态等级、检查特定预订的升级可用性、计算特定奖励兑换所需的积分、检索最近的活动,以及检查特定促销的资格。每个工具都是现有系统或 API 的薄包装,以清晰的描述和参数 schema 暴露给模型。

有趣的设计问题是如何处理写操作。AI 应该能够实际兑换积分、变更预订或应用状态匹配吗?大多数大型企业的保守答案是否定的,每个写操作都通过人工批准步骤。AI 准备行动,提交它供审查,人工提交它。这以自动化换取安全,在 Qantas 品牌标准下,该交换通常是值得的。

另一个有趣的问题是暴露多少工具。诱惑是给 agent 每个可能有用的工具。现实是更多工具混淆模型。十个工具,agent 大多数时候选择正确的。五十个工具,工具选择的失败率明显增长。纪律是为用例暴露最小工具集,并随着 evals 证明价值有意添加工具。

工具设计也被低估。一个参数描述模糊、错误响应不一致的设计糟糕的工具混淆模型。一个描述清晰、参数验证严格、错误消息提供信息的设计良好的工具帮助 agent 从错误中恢复。工具层是产品设计,也是工程。

对 AI 交付来说,更广泛的教训是工具使用是 AI 交付工作与企业技术栈其余部分相交的地方。模型只是大脑。工具是它伸入现有系统的方式。良好设计这些工具,带适当的范围、验证、可观测性,以及人工批准门,是将聊天机器人 demo 转变为真正生产系统的关键。将工具设计视为事后想法的团队发布 demos。将其视为核心工程的团队发布产品。

items.title_en: Single agent vs multi agent, and why multi agent is usually overkill
items.title_zh: 单 agent vs 多 agent,以及为何多 agent 通常是过度
items.body_en:
**Definition**

A single agent is one LLM running in a loop with a set of tools. A multi agent system has multiple LLM instances, often with different roles (planner, researcher, writer, critic), coordinating to complete a task. Multi agent architectures sound elegant and are widely written about. They are rarely the right choice in production.

**Why it matters in delivery**

Multi agent is the architectural pattern most prone to scope creep, cost blowout, and reliability problems. Clients hear about "agent swarms" or "AutoGPT style systems" and ask for them. PMs who can push back with a clear argument for the simpler architecture save weeks of complexity that delivers nothing the client actually needed.

**How it works**

| Architecture | Description | Strength | Weakness |
|---|---|---|---|
| Single agent | One LLM, one prompt, many tools, one loop | Simple, debuggable, cheaper | Can struggle with very complex multi role tasks |
| Sequential pipeline | One LLM call after another, each with a different prompt | Predictable, easy to evaluate per step | Not really "agentic," just a workflow |
| Multi agent with handoffs | Specialised agents pass control to each other (researcher -> writer -> editor) | Modular, clear roles | Higher cost, complex coordination, hard to debug |
| Hierarchical multi agent | A manager agent delegates to worker agents | Handles complex tasks | Compounding error rates, expensive, slow |

The case for single agent: easier to prompt, easier to eval, lower latency, lower cost, fewer failure modes. The case for multi agent: rare, but real, when sub tasks need very different skills (e.g. code execution vs creative writing) or different model tiers (use cheap model for simple steps, expensive model for hard steps).

**PM decision points**

- Can this be done with one well prompted agent and a clear set of tools?
- If multi agent, is each agent doing genuinely different work, or is the split arbitrary?
- How will we debug when something goes wrong across agent handoffs?

**Watch outs**

- Multi agent papers and demos are not production, most do not survive real workloads
- Coordination overhead grows quickly, three agents is much harder than two
- Cost multiplies, multi agent systems often spend 5 to 10x more tokens than necessary

**Takeaway: default to single agent. Only go multi agent when sub tasks need genuinely different capabilities or models.**

**Qantas story**

In a notional Qantas AI architecture, the temptation toward multi agent systems shows up early. A typical pitch goes: build a researcher agent that gathers data, a planner agent that proposes options, a verifier agent that checks constraints, and an executor agent that drafts the output. It sounds modular and elegant. It is almost always the wrong choice.

Consider the disruption recovery use case from earlier. The naive multi agent design has four specialised agents handing off to each other. In practice, this creates several problems. Coordination overhead grows quickly, with each handoff introducing failure points and context loss. Cost multiplies because each agent has its own LLM calls. Debugging is harder because errors can compound across handoffs and the root cause is not always clear. Latency adds up.

The single agent equivalent does all four roles in one loop, with a structured prompt that walks through research, planning, verification, and execution as phases of the same agent's work. The same model, in the same conversation context, performs all four functions. The result is cheaper, faster, easier to debug, and often higher quality because nothing is lost in handoffs.

The case where multi agent earns its complexity at Qantas would be narrow. One example might be an agent that writes code (using a coding optimised model) handing off to an agent that runs tests (using a faster cheaper model with sandboxed execution). The two agents do genuinely different work with different model requirements, and the split is justified. Even there, the modern approach is often a single agent with role specific tools rather than separate agent instances.

The other case is when the sub problems are genuinely parallel. If an agent needs to research multiple options simultaneously (say, four candidate recovery plans), spawning parallel agent instances each working on one option can be faster than serial processing. The pattern is parallelism, not specialisation.

For AI delivery, the practical lesson is that multi agent architectures are popular in conference talks and rare in successful production systems. The default is single agent with good prompting and a clear tool set. Multi agent gets considered only when there is a specific, measurable reason a single agent cannot do the job, and the team can articulate the trade off (cost, complexity) clearly. Most clients who ask for "an agent swarm" because they read about it somewhere accept a single agent solution once the trade offs are explained.
items.body_zh:
**定义**

单 agent 是一个 LLM 在带一组工具的循环中运行。多 agent 系统有多个 LLM 实例,通常具有不同角色 (规划者、研究员、写作者、批评者),协调完成任务。多 agent 架构听起来优雅,被广泛讨论。它们很少是生产中的正确选择。

**为何在交付中重要**

多 agent 是最容易范围蔓延、成本超支和可靠性问题的架构模式。客户听说"agent 群"或"AutoGPT 风格系统",并要求它们。能够用简单架构的清晰论据反驳的 PM 节省了交付客户实际上不需要的任何东西的数周复杂性。

**运作原理**

| 架构 | 描述 | 优势 | 劣势 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 单 agent | 一个 LLM,一个 prompt,许多工具,一个循环 | 简单、可调试、更便宜 | 可能与非常复杂的多角色任务作斗争 |
| 顺序 pipeline | 一个 LLM 调用接一个,每个带不同 prompt | 可预测、容易按步骤评估 | 不是真正的"agentic",只是工作流 |
| 带切换的多 agent | 专门 agent 互相传递控制 (研究员 -> 写作者 -> 编辑) | 模块化、清晰角色 | 更高成本、复杂协调、难以调试 |
| 分层多 agent | 经理 agent 委派给工作者 agents | 处理复杂任务 | 复合错误率、昂贵、慢 |

单 agent 的案例: 更容易 prompt、更容易 eval、更低延迟、更低成本、更少失败模式。多 agent 的案例: 罕见,但真实,当子任务需要非常不同的技能 (例如,代码执行 vs 创意写作) 或不同的模型层级 (简单步骤使用便宜模型,困难步骤使用昂贵模型)。

**PM 决策点**

- 这是否可以用一个良好 prompt 的 agent 和清晰的工具集完成?
- 如果是多 agent,每个 agent 是否真的在做不同的工作,或者拆分是任意的?
- 当出现问题跨 agent 切换时,我们将如何调试?

**注意事项**

- 多 agent 论文和 demos 不是生产,大多数无法在真实工作负载下生存
- 协调开销快速增长,三个 agent 比两个困难得多
- 成本乘以,多 agent 系统经常花费比必要多 5 到 10 倍的 tokens

**要点总结: 默认单 agent。仅当子任务需要真正不同的能力或模型时才使用多 agent。**

**Qantas 案例**

在假设的 Qantas AI 架构中,对多 agent 系统的诱惑早早出现。典型推销说: 构建一个收集数据的研究员 agent、一个提出选项的规划者 agent、一个检查约束的验证者 agent,以及一个起草输出的执行者 agent。它听起来模块化和优雅。它几乎总是错误的选择。

考虑之前的中断恢复用例。天真的多 agent 设计有四个专门 agent 互相切换。在实践中,这创造几个问题。协调开销快速增长,每次切换引入失败点和上下文损失。成本乘以,因为每个 agent 有自己的 LLM 调用。调试更难,因为错误可以跨切换复合,根本原因并不总是清晰。延迟累加。

等效的单 agent 在一个循环中完成所有四个角色,带一个结构化 prompt,引导研究、规划、验证和执行作为同一 agent 工作的阶段。同一模型,在同一对话上下文中,执行所有四个功能。结果更便宜、更快、更容易调试,并且经常质量更高,因为切换中什么都没丢失。

多 agent 在 Qantas 赢得其复杂性的案例将很窄。一个例子可能是一个编写代码的 agent (使用编码优化模型) 切换到一个运行测试的 agent (使用更快更便宜的模型带沙箱执行)。两个 agent 用不同模型要求做真正不同的工作,拆分是合理的。即使在那里,现代方法通常是带角色特定工具的单 agent 而不是单独的 agent 实例。

另一个案例是当子问题真正并行时。如果一个 agent 需要同时研究多个选项 (例如,四个候选恢复计划),生成并行 agent 实例,每个工作于一个选项,可能比串行处理更快。模式是并行性,而不是专业化。

对 AI 交付来说,实践教训是多 agent 架构在会议演讲中受欢迎,在成功的生产系统中罕见。默认是带良好 prompting 和清晰工具集的单 agent。仅当有一个具体的、可衡量的原因单 agent 无法完成工作,并且团队可以清晰地阐述权衡 (成本、复杂性) 时,才考虑多 agent。大多数因为在某处读到而要求"agent 群"的客户,在解释权衡后接受单 agent 解决方案。

items.title_en: Planning, reflection, and self correction patterns
items.title_zh: 规划、反思和自我纠正模式
items.body_en:
**Definition**

Planning, reflection, and self correction are techniques that improve agent reliability by adding explicit reasoning steps. Planning asks the agent to write a plan before acting. Reflection asks the agent to review its own work after acting. Self correction asks the agent to retry or revise when something goes wrong.

**Why it matters in delivery**

Naive agents that just react to each step often fail on complex tasks. They get distracted, take inefficient paths, or stop too early. These three patterns are the most reliable ways to lift agent quality without changing the model. They are cheap to add and most production agents use at least one.

**How it works**

| Pattern | What it does | When to use | Cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| Plan first | Agent writes a step by step plan before executing | Multi step tasks, complex goals | One extra LLM call up front |
| Re plan on failure | When a step fails, agent revises the plan | Tasks with unpredictable obstacles | Extra calls on failure paths |
| Reflection after action | Agent reviews its own output, checks for errors | Quality sensitive tasks, final outputs | Doubles cost on reviewed steps |
| Self correction | Agent retries with a different approach when output is wrong | Coding, structured output, recoverable errors | Extra calls per retry |
| Critique by another agent | A second agent reviews the first agent's work | High stakes outputs | Doubles overall cost |

**Worked example**

Without planning, asked to "research Acme's competitive position":

- Agent calls search ("Acme competitors") -> gets generic list
- Agent calls search ("Acme market share") -> gets one stale figure
- Agent generates a thin summary

With planning:

- Agent writes plan: "1. Identify Acme's industry and segment, 2. List top 3 competitors, 3. Find revenue and market share data, 4. Find recent strategic moves, 5. Synthesise comparative position"
- Agent executes plan step by step
- Agent reflects: "Did I address each point?" If not, retries weak steps
- Output is structured, complete, and traceable

**PM decision points**

- Is the task complex enough that planning adds value, or is the agent already reliable without it?
- What is the quality bar that justifies doubling cost via reflection or critique?
- How do we ensure the agent's plan is not just performance theatre but actually guides execution?

**Watch outs**

- Plans can be wrong, the agent should be allowed to deviate, not slavishly follow a bad plan
- Reflection adds latency, in real time use cases it may be unacceptable
- Self correction loops can run indefinitely, always cap retries

**Takeaway: planning, reflection, and self correction are the cheap quality lifts of agentic design. Add them when reliability matters more than cost or speed.**

**Qantas story**

Reflection and planning patterns are particularly valuable in Qantas AI use cases where the cost of getting it wrong is high. Take the disruption recovery agent from earlier. A naive version reacts to each step in isolation and can produce recovery plans that look reasonable but miss critical constraints. Adding planning and reflection transforms the output.

The pattern works as follows. When a disruption is detected, the agent first writes a structured plan: "I will (1) identify all affected flights and downstream rotations, (2) classify each flight by impact, (3) identify constraints (crew duty, aircraft availability, slot rules), (4) propose recovery options per affected flight, (5) verify each option against constraints, (6) rank options by total cost and customer impact, (7) generate a recovery summary." The plan is visible to the operations controller before execution.

The agent then works through the plan. After each major step, a reflection prompt asks "have I addressed everything required by this step, and have I introduced any inconsistencies with earlier steps." The reflection is a separate model call, and it adds latency and cost, but it catches errors that single shot reasoning misses.

At the end, a final reflection asks "is this recovery plan internally consistent, does it respect all constraints, and would I confidently present it to a duty manager." If the reflection identifies issues, the agent revises before presenting.

The cost of this discipline is real. Planning and reflection roughly double the LLM cost per task. The benefit is also real. In high stakes contexts like disruption recovery, the quality lift from these patterns is the difference between a tool that operations controllers trust and one they ignore. Trust is the currency of AI adoption in operational environments.

The interesting failure mode is performance theatre, where the agent writes plans and reflections that look thorough but do not actually shape its behaviour. The agent says "I will check crew duty time limits" and then proceeds to recommend a swap that violates them. The defence is to have plans and reflections produce structured output that downstream code actually validates, not just freeform text that nobody reads.

For AI delivery, the lesson is that planning and reflection are the cheap quality lifts of agentic design. They double cost but often more than double quality on hard tasks. The right framing for clients is to position them as the difference between a draft and a reviewed draft, not as fancy AI patterns. Operations leaders understand the value of reviewed work, and that framing builds trust faster than technical descriptions.
items.body_zh:
**定义**

规划、反思和自我纠正是通过添加显式推理步骤来提高 agent 可靠性的技术。规划要求 agent 在行动之前写一个计划。反思要求 agent 在行动之后审查自己的工作。自我纠正要求 agent 在出错时重试或修订。

**为何在交付中重要**

仅对每一步反应的天真 agent 经常在复杂任务上失败。它们分心、走低效的路径,或过早停止。这三种模式是在不改变模型的情况下提升 agent 质量的最可靠方式。它们添加便宜,大多数生产 agent 至少使用一种。

**运作原理**

| 模式 | 它做什么 | 何时使用 | 成本 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 先规划 | Agent 在执行前写一步一步的计划 | 多步任务、复杂目标 | 一次额外的 LLM 调用预先 |
| 失败时重新规划 | 当步骤失败时,agent 修订计划 | 带不可预测障碍的任务 | 失败路径上的额外调用 |
| 行动后反思 | Agent 审查自己的输出,检查错误 | 质量敏感的任务,最终输出 | 在审查步骤上成本翻倍 |
| 自我纠正 | 当输出错误时,Agent 用不同方法重试 | 编码、结构化输出、可恢复错误 | 每次重试的额外调用 |
| 另一个 agent 的批评 | 第二个 agent 审查第一个的工作 | 高风险输出 | 整体成本翻倍 |

**举例**

没有规划,被要求"研究 Acme 的竞争位置":

- Agent 调用搜索 ("Acme 竞争对手") -> 得到通用列表
- Agent 调用搜索 ("Acme 市场份额") -> 得到一个过时的数字
- Agent 生成一个薄的摘要

有规划:

- Agent 写计划: "1. 识别 Acme 的行业和细分市场,2. 列出前 3 个竞争对手,3. 找到收入和市场份额数据,4. 找到最近的战略举措,5. 综合比较位置"
- Agent 按计划逐步执行
- Agent 反思: "我是否解决了每一点?"如果没有,重试薄弱的步骤
- 输出是结构化的、完整的,并且可追溯

**PM 决策点**

- 任务是否足够复杂,规划增加价值,或者 agent 在没有它的情况下已经可靠?
- 通过反思或批评使成本翻倍的质量门槛是什么?
- 我们如何确保 agent 的计划不仅是表演而是实际指导执行?

**注意事项**

- 计划可能错误,agent 应被允许偏离,而不是奴隶般遵循糟糕的计划
- 反思增加延迟,在实时用例中可能不可接受
- 自我纠正循环可以无限运行,总是限制重试

**要点总结: 规划、反思和自我纠正是 agentic 设计的廉价质量提升。当可靠性比成本或速度更重要时添加它们。**

**Qantas 案例**

反思和规划模式在 Qantas AI 用例中特别有价值,在那里出错的成本很高。以之前的中断恢复 agent 为例。天真的版本对每一步孤立反应,可能产生看起来合理但错过关键约束的恢复计划。添加规划和反思转变输出。

模式如下工作。当检测到中断时,agent 首先写一个结构化计划: "我将 (1) 识别所有受影响的航班和下游轮换,(2) 按影响分类每个航班,(3) 识别约束 (机组值勤、飞机可用性、时刻规则),(4) 为每个受影响航班提出恢复选项,(5) 根据约束验证每个选项,(6) 按总成本和客户影响对选项排名,(7) 生成恢复摘要。"计划对运营控制员在执行前可见。

然后 agent 通过计划工作。在每个主要步骤之后,反思 prompt 问"我是否解决了这一步要求的一切,以及我是否引入了与早期步骤的不一致"。反思是单独的模型调用,它增加延迟和成本,但它捕捉单次推理错过的错误。

最后,最终反思问"这个恢复计划在内部一致吗,它是否尊重所有约束,我会自信地将它呈现给值班经理吗"。如果反思识别问题,agent 在呈现之前修订。

这种纪律的成本是真实的。规划和反思大致使每任务的 LLM 成本翻倍。好处也是真实的。在像中断恢复这样的高风险情境中,从这些模式的质量提升是运营控制员信任的工具和他们忽略的工具之间的区别。信任是运营环境中 AI 采用的货币。

有趣的失败模式是性能表演,agent 写看起来彻底但实际上不塑造其行为的计划和反思。Agent 说"我将检查机组值勤时间限制",然后继续推荐违反它们的调换。防御是让计划和反思产生下游代码实际验证的结构化输出,而不仅仅是没有人阅读的自由形式文本。

对 AI 交付来说,启示是规划和反思是 agentic 设计的廉价质量提升。它们使成本翻倍,但经常在硬任务上使质量提升超过两倍。对客户的正确框架是将它们定位为草稿和审查草稿之间的区别,而不是花哨的 AI 模式。运营领导者理解审查工作的价值,这种框架比技术描述更快地建立信任。

items.title_en: Where agents break: long horizons, error compounding, cost blowouts
items.title_zh: Agent 在哪里崩溃: 长视野、错误复合、成本爆炸
items.body_en:
**Definition**

Agents fail in characteristic ways that are different from single LLM call failures. The three most common are: long horizon failures (agent loses the thread on tasks with many steps), error compounding (small errors snowball across steps), and cost blowouts (agents run for far more steps than expected). Understanding these failure modes is what separates teams that ship reliable agents from teams that abandon agent projects.

**Why it matters in delivery**

Almost every agent project hits these failure modes in production. PMs who recognise the pattern can scope around them and set guardrails early. PMs who do not get blindsided in week three when costs are 5x forecast and tasks are completing 60 percent of the time.

**How it works**

| Failure mode | What happens | Why | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Long horizon failure | Agent forgets the original goal after many steps | Context fills with intermediate results, original task drifts | Re inject goal each iteration, summarise old steps, hard step limit |
| Error compounding | Small mistakes accumulate, final output is badly wrong | Each step's small error feeds the next step | Verification at each step, narrower tool surface, eval per step |
| Cost blowout | Agent runs 50 steps for a task that should take 5 | Inefficient loops, agent over thinks, retries pile up | Step limit, cost cap per task, route easy tasks away from agent |
| Tool misuse | Agent calls wrong tool or wrong arguments | Too many tools, vague descriptions | Fewer tools, clearer descriptions, validation |
| Infinite loops | Agent gets stuck retrying the same thing | No stop condition, model confidence stays high | Detect repeated states, force escalation |
| Silent failure | Agent reports success but did not complete | No verification step, hallucinated success | Tool result validation, completion checks |

**Worked example, error compounding**

Step 1: Agent retrieves customer record. Correct, but uses outdated cached data.

Step 2: Agent looks up account based on step 1 data. Finds the wrong account.

Step 3: Agent summarises account activity. Activity is real but for the wrong account.

Step 4: Agent emails the customer. Email is fluent, polite, and entirely wrong.

No single step looked broken. The error compounded silently.

**PM decision points**

- What is the maximum acceptable cost and time per task, and is the agent enforcing it?
- How does the system handle tasks that hit limits, escalate, fail gracefully, retry?
- Where are we verifying intermediate results vs trusting them blindly?

**Watch outs**

- Demos always hit best case, production hits worst case, plan for both
- Cost monitoring needs to be at task level, not just monthly aggregate
- Long horizon tasks (over 20 steps) are at the edge of what current models do reliably, scope accordingly

**Takeaway: agents fail in compounding ways. Cap steps, cap cost, verify results, and have a human escalation path from day one.**

**Qantas story**

Agent failure modes show up in interesting ways at Qantas scale. Consider the disruption recovery agent again, in production. The expected behaviour is that each recovery task completes in five to ten agent steps, costs about AUD 0.50 in model calls, and produces a coherent recovery plan within ninety seconds.

The actual production behaviour, in the first weeks of any such system, would likely include the following failure modes. A small percentage of tasks involve unusually complex disruptions and the agent loops well beyond the expected step count, running fifty or more steps and costing AUD 15 per task. Some tasks get stuck retrying the same retrieval call because the underlying data is incomplete and the agent does not recognise it. Some tasks produce confidently wrong outputs because an earlier step retrieved stale data and every subsequent step compounded the error. Some tasks silently fail by reporting success while having skipped a critical constraint check.

Each of these is a known agent failure pattern, and each has a known mitigation. Hard step limits cap runaway loops. Cost limits per task prevent budget surprises. Detection of repeated tool calls with same parameters catches stuck loops. Verification steps after each major decision catch error compounding. Schema validation on agent outputs catches silent failures.

The interesting organisational point is who notices these failures. Cost monitoring at the team level catches the first failure mode within hours. Customer service tickets about wrong recovery decisions catch the second mode within days. Audit reviews catch the third and fourth modes within weeks. Each mode has a different surface area, and the observability strategy needs to cover all of them.

The other lesson is that agent failure rates depend heavily on the difficulty distribution of the workload. A pilot with curated test cases looks great. Production with the full long tail of real disruptions looks much worse. The gap between pilot success and production reality is often 20 to 30 percentage points on task completion rate. Teams that plan for this gap, with conservative rollout, graceful escalation to human handlers, and aggressive monitoring, survive the first month. Teams that do not, often pause the rollout and lose months rebuilding confidence.

For AI delivery, the takeaway is that agents fail in compounding, expensive, sometimes silent ways. The mitigations are well known and not optional. Hard limits on steps and cost. Verification at every meaningful decision point. Observability that surfaces both successful tasks and the cost distribution. A clear escalation path to humans when limits are hit. Teams that build these in from the first version ship agents that survive contact with production. Teams that bolt them on after the first incident lose trust quickly and rarely recover it.
items.body_zh:
**定义**

Agent 失败模式以与单 LLM 调用失败不同的特征方式出现。最常见的三种是: 长视野失败 (agent 在多步任务上失去线索)、错误复合 (小错误跨步骤滚雪球),以及成本爆炸 (agent 运行的步骤比预期多得多)。理解这些失败模式是发布可靠 agent 的团队与放弃 agent 项目的团队之间的区别。

**为何在交付中重要**

几乎每个 agent 项目在生产中都遇到这些失败模式。识别模式的 PM 可以围绕它们确定范围并尽早设置护栏。不识别的 PM 在第三周被打蒙,当成本是预测的 5 倍,任务完成率为 60% 时。

**运作原理**

| 失败模式 | 发生了什么 | 为什么 | 缓解 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 长视野失败 | Agent 在许多步骤后忘记原始目标 | 上下文填满中间结果,原始任务漂移 | 每次迭代重新注入目标、总结旧步骤、硬步骤限制 |
| 错误复合 | 小错误累积,最终输出严重错误 | 每一步的小错误进入下一步 | 每步验证、更窄的工具表面、按步骤 eval |
| 成本爆炸 | Agent 为应该用 5 步完成的任务运行 50 步 | 低效循环、agent 过度思考、重试堆积 | 步骤限制、每任务成本上限、将简单任务路由远离 agent |
| 工具误用 | Agent 调用错误的工具或错误的参数 | 太多工具、模糊的描述 | 更少的工具、更清晰的描述、验证 |
| 无限循环 | Agent 卡在重试相同的事情 | 无停止条件、模型置信度保持高 | 检测重复状态、强制升级 |
| 静默失败 | Agent 报告成功但没有完成 | 无验证步骤、幻觉的成功 | 工具结果验证、完成检查 |

**举例,错误复合**

步骤 1: Agent 检索客户记录。正确,但使用过时的缓存数据。

步骤 2: Agent 基于步骤 1 的数据查找账户。找到错误的账户。

步骤 3: Agent 总结账户活动。活动是真实的,但是错误的账户。

步骤 4: Agent 发送电子邮件给客户。电子邮件流畅、礼貌,完全错误。

没有一个步骤看起来损坏。错误静默复合。

**PM 决策点**

- 每任务可接受的最大成本和时间是多少,agent 是否在强制它?
- 系统如何处理达到限制的任务,升级、优雅失败、重试?
- 我们在哪里验证中间结果与盲目信任它们?

**注意事项**

- Demos 总是命中最佳情况,生产命中最坏情况,为两者计划
- 成本监控需要在任务级别,而不仅仅是每月聚合
- 长视野任务 (超过 20 步) 处于当前模型可靠完成的边缘,相应地确定范围

**要点总结: Agent 以复合方式失败。限制步骤,限制成本,验证结果,并从第一天起有人工升级路径。**

**Qantas 案例**

Agent 失败模式在 Qantas 规模上以有趣的方式出现。再考虑生产中的中断恢复 agent。预期行为是每个恢复任务在五到十个 agent 步骤中完成,在模型调用上花费约 0.50 澳元,并在九十秒内产生一个连贯的恢复计划。

任何这样系统的实际生产行为,在头几周,可能包括以下失败模式。一小部分任务涉及异常复杂的中断,agent 远远超过预期的步骤计数循环,运行五十或更多步骤,每任务花费 15 澳元。一些任务卡在重试相同的检索调用,因为底层数据不完整,agent 不识别它。一些任务产生自信地错误的输出,因为较早的步骤检索了过时的数据,每个后续步骤复合了错误。一些任务通过报告成功而跳过关键约束检查静默失败。

这些每一个都是已知的 agent 失败模式,每一个都有已知的缓解。硬步骤限制限制失控循环。每任务成本限制防止预算意外。检测带相同参数的重复工具调用捕捉卡住的循环。每个主要决策后的验证步骤捕捉错误复合。Agent 输出的 schema 验证捕捉静默失败。

有趣的组织点是谁注意到这些失败。团队级别的成本监控在几小时内捕捉第一个失败模式。关于错误恢复决策的客户服务工单在几天内捕捉第二个模式。审计审查在几周内捕捉第三和第四个模式。每种模式有不同的表面区域,可观测性策略需要覆盖所有这些。

另一个教训是 agent 失败率严重依赖工作负载的难度分布。带精选测试用例的试点看起来很棒。带真实中断完整长尾的生产看起来糟糕得多。试点成功和生产现实之间的差距通常是任务完成率上 20 到 30 个百分点。计划这种差距的团队,带保守推出、对人工处理者的优雅升级,以及积极监控,在第一个月内生存。不这样做的团队,经常暂停推出,失去重建信心的数月。

对 AI 交付来说,要点是 agent 以复合的、昂贵的,有时静默的方式失败。缓解是众所周知的,不可选。对步骤和成本的硬限制。每个有意义决策点的验证。表面成功任务和成本分布的可观测性。当限制被达到时对人类的清晰升级路径。从第一版本就构建这些的团队发布在与生产接触后生存的 agents。在第一次事件后才把它们螺栓固定的团队迅速失去信任,很少恢复。

subtitle_en: Prompting vs RAG vs fine tuning, SFT, DPO, LoRA, distillation

items.title_en: Prompting vs RAG vs fine tuning: the decision tree
items.title_zh: Prompting vs RAG vs fine tuning: 决策树
items.body_en:
**Definition**

These are the three main ways to make an LLM behave the way you want for a specific use case. Prompting changes the instructions you send to the model. RAG provides external information at query time. Fine tuning modifies the model itself by training it on your data. They solve different problems and are often used together, but the order matters.

**Why it matters in delivery**

Picking the wrong one wastes weeks and tens of thousands of dollars. The most common mistake is jumping to fine tuning when prompting or RAG would have worked. The second most common mistake is using RAG when prompting alone was enough. PMs who know the decision tree make defensible architecture calls quickly.

**How it works**

The simple decision sequence:

1. Try prompting first. If the model can do it with the right instructions and examples, stop.
2. If the model lacks knowledge (your data, recent data), add RAG.
3. If the model still cannot reliably produce the right format, tone, or behaviour after good prompting, then consider fine tuning.

| Approach | Solves | Does not solve | Effort | Cost |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Prompting | Behaviour, format, tone, simple task framing | Lack of knowledge, very specialised domains | Hours | Just inference cost |
| RAG | Private data, fresh data, citations, large knowledge bases | Style consistency, format reliability, latency | Days to weeks | Inference plus retrieval infra |
| Fine tuning | Style, format consistency, narrow specialised tasks, smaller model matching larger | Knowledge gaps (RAG does that better), rapidly changing data | Weeks | Training plus higher inference cost |

**Worked example**

Client request: "Make the model answer support questions like our top agent Sarah."

Wrong path: jump to fine tuning on Sarah's transcripts. Three months, USD 80K, mediocre results.

Right path:

1. Prompting: "You are a customer support agent. Tone is warm but direct. Always confirm understanding before answering. Here are 5 examples of Sarah's style." Test. Often gets 80 percent of the way.
2. RAG: add Sarah's knowledge base, product docs, past tickets. Gets to 95 percent.
3. Only then consider fine tuning if the remaining 5 percent is worth the cost.

**PM decision points**

- Has the team genuinely exhausted prompting before recommending anything more complex?
- Is the gap a knowledge problem (RAG) or a behaviour problem (fine tuning)?
- Can the client articulate what fine tuning would deliver that prompting plus RAG cannot?

**Watch outs**

- Clients hear "fine tuning" and assume it is the sophisticated answer, it is usually not
- Fine tuning locks you to a model version, every upgrade costs another training cycle
- The decision should be data driven, build an eval first, then test each approach against it

**Takeaway: prompt first, retrieve second, fine tune last. The default sequence saves most projects from over engineering.**

**Qantas story**

Within Qantas, the decision tree between prompting, RAG, and fine tuning plays out across many use cases, and the most expensive mistakes happen when teams jump to fine tuning too early.

Consider a hypothetical use case: generating Qantas brand consistent marketing copy for route specific promotions. The naive scoping says "fine tune a model on our existing marketing copy so it sounds like us." The budget is AUD 80K and the timeline is three months.

A disciplined scoping process tests each step of the decision tree first. Step one, prompting. A strong system prompt with five example pieces of Qantas marketing copy, clear tone guidelines (warm, optimistic, never overpromising), and the specific route context produces output that hits the brand voice for the vast majority of cases. Test with editors, get qualitative feedback, refine the system prompt.

Step two, RAG. For copy that references specific Qantas content (route history, frequent flyer benefits, destination experiences), add retrieval over the Qantas marketing content library. This grounds claims in actual brand approved language and prevents hallucinated facts about routes or services.

After steps one and two, evaluate honestly. If the output meets the quality bar, ship it. If there is a residual gap, characterise it. Is it a brand voice issue (more example tuning might fix it), a knowledge issue (better retrieval would fix it), or a format issue (fine tuning might fix it)?

In most cases like this, fine tuning is unnecessary. The combination of strong prompting and good retrieval produces output indistinguishable from brand approved copy. The AUD 80K fine tuning budget is redirected to evaluation infrastructure, content governance for the retrieval source, and ongoing prompt refinement. The timeline shrinks from three months to four weeks.

The cases where fine tuning genuinely earns its place at Qantas would be narrower. One example might be matching a very specific format like operational notices to crew, where the structure is rigid, the vocabulary is specialised, and the volume justifies the engineering. Even there, the right starting point is exhausted prompting plus RAG, and fine tuning is the last resort, not the first.

For AI delivery, the broader insight is that the decision tree exists precisely because skipping it is so common and so expensive. Most enterprise AI projects that "need fine tuning" actually need better prompting and retrieval. The delivery practitioner who can walk a client through the tree calmly, with eval data at each step, saves the client real money and ships faster. The client appreciates this, and it sets up future projects to be scoped the same way.
items.body_zh:
**定义**

这是让 LLM 以你想要的方式为特定用例行为的三种主要方式。Prompting 改变你发送给模型的指令。RAG 在查询时提供外部信息。Fine tuning 通过在你的数据上训练来修改模型本身。它们解决不同的问题,并且经常一起使用,但顺序很重要。

**为何在交付中重要**

选错一个浪费数周和数万美元。最常见的错误是在 prompting 或 RAG 本来可以工作时跳到 fine tuning。第二个最常见的错误是在仅 prompting 就足够时使用 RAG。了解决策树的 PM 快速做出可辩护的架构决定。

**运作原理**

简单的决策序列:

1. 首先尝试 prompting。如果模型可以用正确的指令和示例完成,停止。
2. 如果模型缺乏知识 (你的数据、最近的数据),添加 RAG。
3. 如果模型在良好 prompting 后仍然无法可靠地产生正确的格式、语气或行为,那么考虑 fine tuning。

| 方法 | 解决 | 不解决 | 努力 | 成本 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Prompting | 行为、格式、语气、简单任务框架 | 缺乏知识、非常专业的领域 | 数小时 | 仅推理成本 |
| RAG | 私有数据、新鲜数据、引用、大型知识库 | 风格一致性、格式可靠性、延迟 | 数天到数周 | 推理加检索基础设施 |
| Fine tuning | 风格、格式一致性、狭窄专业任务、匹配较大模型的较小模型 | 知识差距 (RAG 更好)、快速变化的数据 | 数周 | 训练加更高的推理成本 |

**举例**

客户请求: "让模型像我们的顶级代理 Sarah 一样回答支持问题。"

错误路径: 跳到 Sarah 的转录上的 fine tuning。三个月,8 万美元,平庸的结果。

正确路径:

1. Prompting: "你是客户支持代理。语气温暖但直接。在回答前总是确认理解。这里是 Sarah 风格的 5 个示例。"测试。通常达到 80% 的路径。
2. RAG: 添加 Sarah 的知识库、产品文档、过去的工单。达到 95%。
3. 只有那时才考虑 fine tuning,如果剩余 5% 值得成本。

**PM 决策点**

- 在推荐任何更复杂的东西之前,团队是否真正穷尽了 prompting?
- 差距是知识问题 (RAG) 还是行为问题 (fine tuning)?
- 客户能否阐明 fine tuning 将交付什么是 prompting 加 RAG 不能?

**注意事项**

- 客户听到"fine tuning"并假设它是复杂的答案,通常不是
- Fine tuning 把你锁定到一个模型版本,每次升级都需要另一个训练周期
- 决策应是数据驱动的,先构建 eval,然后针对它测试每种方法

**要点总结: 先 prompt,然后 retrieve,最后 fine tune。默认序列拯救大多数项目免于过度工程化。**

**Qantas 案例**

在 Qantas 内部,prompting、RAG 和 fine tuning 之间的决策树在许多用例中演出,最昂贵的错误发生在团队过早跳到 fine tuning 时。

考虑一个假设的 Qantas 团队: 为特定路线促销生成 Qantas 品牌一致的营销文案。天真的需求确定说"在我们现有的营销文案上 fine tune 模型,使它听起来像我们"。预算是 8 万澳元,时间表是三个月。

有纪律的需求确定过程首先测试决策树的每一步。步骤一,prompting。带五个 Qantas 营销文案示例的强 system prompt、清晰的语气指南 (温暖、乐观、从不过度承诺),以及特定路线上下文,产生在绝大多数情况下命中品牌声音的输出。与编辑测试,获得定性反馈,改进 system prompt。

步骤二,RAG。对引用特定 Qantas 内容 (路线历史、frequent flyer 利益、目的地体验) 的文案,添加在 Qantas 营销内容库上的检索。这将声明锚定在实际品牌批准的语言中,并防止关于路线或服务的捏造事实。

在步骤一和步骤二之后,诚实地评估。如果输出达到质量门槛,发布它。如果有残余差距,描述它。它是品牌声音问题 (更多示例调整可能修复它)、知识问题 (更好的检索会修复它),还是格式问题 (fine tuning 可能修复它)?

在像这样的大多数情况下,fine tuning 是不必要的。强 prompting 和良好检索的组合产生与品牌批准文案无法区分的输出。8 万澳元的 fine tuning 预算被重新引导到评估基础设施、检索源的内容治理,以及持续 prompt 改进。时间表从三个月缩短到四周。

在 Qantas fine tuning 真正赢得位置的案例将更窄。一个例子可能是匹配像给机组的运营通知这样的非常特定格式,在那里结构严格,词汇专业化,量证明工程合理。即使在那里,正确的起点是穷尽 prompting 加 RAG,fine tuning 是最后手段,而不是第一个。

对 AI 交付来说,更广泛的洞察是决策树存在恰恰是因为跳过它如此常见和如此昂贵。大多数"需要 fine tuning"的企业 AI 项目实际上需要更好的 prompting 和检索。能够冷静地走客户通过树、在每一步带 eval 数据的交付从业者节省客户真正的金钱并更快发布。客户欣赏这一点,这为未来项目以同样的方式被确定范围奠定基础。

items.title_en: Supervised fine tuning, preference tuning (RLHF, DPO), in concept
items.title_zh: 监督 fine tuning,偏好调整 (RLHF、DPO),概念上
items.body_en:
**Definition**

There are two main families of fine tuning that customers can apply. Supervised fine tuning (SFT) trains the model on input output pairs, showing it the right answer for each input. Preference tuning (RLHF, DPO) trains the model on comparisons, showing it which of two responses is better. These are the same techniques the labs use during post training, applied to your specific data.

**Why it matters in delivery**

Clients ask "can we fine tune?" without knowing what kind. The two types solve different problems. SFT teaches the model what to produce. Preference tuning teaches the model what to prefer. Knowing the difference lets you scope realistically and explain trade offs to the client.

**How it works**

| Method | What it teaches | Data needed | Effort |
|---|---|---|---|
| Supervised fine tuning (SFT) | "For this input, produce this output" | 500 to 10,000+ labelled examples | Moderate, well supported in APIs |
| RLHF (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback) | Prefer responses humans rate higher | Thousands of preference comparisons plus reward model | Heavy, rarely done by customers |
| DPO (Direct Preference Optimisation) | Prefer responses humans rate higher, simpler than RLHF | Pairs of preferred vs rejected responses | Moderate, increasingly available |
| Constitutional / rule based | Prefer responses that follow rules | Rule set plus pairs | Specialised, lab grade |

For most enterprise customers, SFT is the only realistic option. Preference tuning is available via some APIs but requires preference data most teams do not have.

**Worked example**

SFT data looks like:

```
Input: "Summarise this medical record for the GP referral letter"
Output: "[example summary in the exact format the client wants]"
```

You provide 1,000 examples like this. The model learns the pattern.

DPO data looks like:

```
Input: "Draft a renewal email to a frustrated customer"
Chosen response: "[good response]"
Rejected response: "[mediocre response]"
```

You provide 500 pairs. The model learns to prefer the chosen style.

**PM decision points**

- Does the client have the right kind of data, labelled pairs for SFT, preference comparisons for DPO?
- Is the goal to teach a specific output (SFT) or to nudge style (preference)?
- Is preference tuning even available on the chosen model, many APIs only support SFT?

**Watch outs**

- SFT requires high quality examples, garbage in garbage out is amplified
- Preference tuning needs preference data, which is expensive to collect well
- Both methods need an eval set the fine tuning data has never seen, otherwise you cannot measure generalisation

**Takeaway: SFT is the realistic fine tuning option for most enterprise projects. Preference tuning exists but rarely fits client data and budget.**

**Qantas story**

The two main fine tuning approaches available to Qantas would be supervised fine tuning (SFT) and direct preference optimisation (DPO), and the choice depends on what kind of data the team actually has.

SFT works when there is a corpus of input output pairs that represent the desired behaviour. For example, the Qantas customer communications team has thousands of historical delay notifications they have written over the years, each paired with the underlying flight disruption details. That is exactly the right shape for SFT. The team could fine tune a smaller model on these pairs and end up with a model that produces notifications in the precise Qantas voice, with consistent structure, appropriate tone, and the specific phrasings the brand team prefers. The cost is moderate, the data is already labelled, and the result is a specialist model for that task.

DPO requires preference data, pairs of outputs where humans have indicated which one is better. This is much harder to produce. Most Qantas teams have outputs that were produced (the historical delay notifications) but no parallel set of rejected alternatives. Creating preference data retroactively means generating multiple candidate outputs, having brand or content reviewers grade them, and assembling pairs. This is expensive enough that DPO is rarely the right approach for an enterprise team that does not already have preference data flowing from another source.

The more interesting practical pattern at Qantas would be to fine tune small models with SFT for high volume narrow tasks, leaving the flagship API model for hard general tasks. A fine tuned 8B model on customer service classification, running on Bedrock with provisioned throughput, can handle millions of classifications per month at a cost that is dramatically lower than flagship API consumption. The classification accuracy can be tuned to within a percentage point or two of flagship quality on the specific task. The savings are real and the engineering is well understood.

The cases where this does not work are also worth knowing. Fine tuning teaches style, format, and narrow task behaviour. It does not reliably teach new facts. If the goal is for the model to "know about Qantas products and policies," fine tuning is the wrong tool. RAG over current product documentation is the right tool. Mixing these up is a common scoping mistake.

For AI delivery, the lesson is that fine tuning is a real tool in the toolbox for specific, well defined situations. The discipline is to know what shape of data you have, what kind of behaviour you are trying to teach, and whether the task and volume justify the engineering. Most enterprise teams ask for fine tuning because it sounds sophisticated and end up not needing it. The minority who genuinely need it benefit from doing it well, with proper eval discipline.
items.body_zh:
**定义**

客户可以应用的两种主要 fine tuning 家族。监督 fine tuning (SFT) 在输入输出对上训练模型,显示每个输入的正确答案。偏好调整 (RLHF、DPO) 在比较上训练模型,显示两个响应中哪个更好。这些是实验室在 post training 期间使用的相同技术,应用于你的特定数据。

**为何在交付中重要**

客户问"我们可以 fine tune 吗",不知道是哪种。两种类型解决不同的问题。SFT 教模型生成什么。偏好调整教模型偏好什么。了解差异让你能够实际地确定范围,并向客户解释权衡。

**运作原理**

| 方法 | 它教什么 | 需要的数据 | 努力 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 监督 fine tuning (SFT) | "对于这个输入,产生这个输出" | 500 到 10,000+ 个标注示例 | 中等,API 中良好支持 |
| RLHF (从人类反馈强化学习) | 偏好人类评分更高的响应 | 数千个偏好比较加奖励模型 | 重,客户很少做 |
| DPO (直接偏好优化) | 偏好人类评分更高的响应,比 RLHF 简单 | 偏好响应与拒绝响应的对 | 中等,越来越可用 |
| 宪法 / 基于规则 | 偏好遵循规则的响应 | 规则集加对 | 专业化,实验室级别 |

对大多数企业客户,SFT 是唯一现实的选项。偏好调整通过一些 API 可用,但需要大多数团队没有的偏好数据。

**举例**

SFT 数据看起来像:

```
输入: "总结这份医疗记录用于 GP 推荐信"
输出: "[精确格式中客户想要的示例摘要]"
```

你提供 1,000 个这样的示例。模型学习模式。

DPO 数据看起来像:

```
输入: "为沮丧的客户起草续约电子邮件"
选择的响应: "[好的响应]"
被拒绝的响应: "[平庸的响应]"
```

你提供 500 个对。模型学会偏好选择的风格。

**PM 决策点**

- 客户是否有正确类型的数据,SFT 的标注对、DPO 的偏好比较?
- 目标是教特定输出 (SFT) 还是微调风格 (偏好)?
- 偏好调整在所选模型上是否可用,许多 API 仅支持 SFT?

**注意事项**

- SFT 需要高质量示例,垃圾进垃圾出被放大
- 偏好调整需要偏好数据,这很贵难以收集得好
- 两种方法都需要 fine tuning 数据从未见过的 eval 集,否则你无法衡量泛化

**要点总结: SFT 是大多数企业项目现实的 fine tuning 选项。偏好调整存在,但很少适合客户数据和预算。**

**Qantas 案例**

可供 Qantas 的两种主要 fine tuning 方法将是监督 fine tuning (SFT) 和直接偏好优化 (DPO),选择取决于团队实际拥有什么样的数据。

SFT 在有代表所需行为的输入输出对语料库时工作。例如,Qantas 客户沟通团队多年来写了数千条历史延误通知,每条都与底层航班中断详情配对。那正是 SFT 的正确形状。团队可以在这些对上 fine tune 较小的模型,最终得到一个以精确 Qantas 声音、一致结构、适当语气和品牌团队偏好的特定措辞产生通知的模型。成本适中,数据已标注,结果是该任务的专家模型。

DPO 需要偏好数据,人类已经指出哪个更好的输出对。这要难得多产生。大多数 Qantas 团队有产生的输出 (历史延误通知),但没有平行的拒绝替代方案集。回顾性地创建偏好数据意味着生成多个候选输出、让品牌或内容审查员评分,并组装对。这足够贵,以至于 DPO 很少是不已经从其他来源流入偏好数据的企业团队的正确方法。

Qantas 更有趣的实际模式将是用 SFT fine tune 小型模型用于高量窄任务,将旗舰 API 模型留给困难的通用任务。在客户服务分类上 fine tuned 的 8B 模型,在 Bedrock 上运行带预配吞吐量,可以以比旗舰 API 消费显著低得多的成本每月处理数百万分类。分类准确性可以调到具体任务上旗舰质量的一两个百分点内。节省是真实的,工程是众所周知的。

这不起作用的案例也值得了解。Fine tuning 教风格、格式和窄任务行为。它不可靠地教新事实。如果目标是让模型"了解 Qantas 产品和政策",fine tuning 是错误的工具。在当前产品文档上的 RAG 是正确的工具。混淆这些是常见的需求确定错误。

对 AI 交付来说,启示是 fine tuning 是工具箱中针对特定、定义良好情况的真正工具。纪律是知道你有什么形状的数据、你试图教什么样的行为,以及任务和量是否证明工程合理。大多数企业团队要求 fine tuning,因为它听起来复杂,最终发现不需要。真正需要它的少数受益于做得好,带适当的 eval 纪律。

items.title_en: LoRA and parameter efficient fine tuning, why it matters for cost
items.title_zh: LoRA 和参数高效 fine tuning,为何它对成本重要
items.body_en:
**Definition**

LoRA (Low Rank Adaptation) is the most common form of parameter efficient fine tuning. Instead of updating all the weights of a large model during training, LoRA freezes the original weights and trains a small set of additional weights, typically 0.1 to 1 percent of the total. The result behaves like a fine tuned model but is far cheaper to train and serve.

**Why it matters in delivery**

Full fine tuning of a large model is expensive, slow, and produces a separate full copy of the model that you have to host. LoRA changes the economics. You can fine tune large open weight models on a single GPU in hours instead of weeks on a cluster. You can also stack multiple LoRA adaptations for different clients on top of the same base model, dramatically lowering serving costs. This is the technique that makes self hosted fine tuning practical for most teams.

**How it works**

| Method | What gets trained | Training cost | Serving cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| Full fine tuning | All model weights | Very high (cluster, days to weeks) | Full size model |
| LoRA | Small adapter matrices (0.1 to 1% of weights) | Low (single GPU, hours) | Base model plus tiny adapter |
| QLoRA | LoRA on a quantised (compressed) model | Lowest (consumer GPU possible) | Even lower memory |
| Prefix tuning | Trained virtual tokens prepended to input | Low | Adds tokens to context |

Visually, full fine tuning is like rewriting the model. LoRA is like attaching a small "personality module" that modifies the model's behaviour at inference time without changing the underlying weights.

The serving benefit is huge: you can swap LoRA adapters per request, so one base model can serve dozens of fine tuned variants without loading separate models into memory.

**PM decision points**

- Is the project doing open weight fine tuning where LoRA applies, or closed API fine tuning where the provider handles it?
- Will the system serve multiple fine tuned variants, where LoRA's adapter swapping shines?
- Has the team tested LoRA against full fine tuning, the quality gap is often negligible?

**Watch outs**

- LoRA quality is excellent for style and tone, slightly weaker for teaching genuinely new knowledge
- LoRA adapters are model specific, switching base models means redoing the work
- Closed API fine tuning often uses LoRA under the hood without telling you, which is fine

**Takeaway: LoRA makes fine tuning practical. Use it as the default for self hosted fine tuning unless there is a clear reason to go full parameter.**

**Qantas story**

If Qantas were to operate fine tuned models in production at scale, LoRA would almost certainly be the right approach. The economics make the difference between fine tuning being a curiosity and being a practical production pattern.

Consider the hypothetical Qantas customer service classification use case from earlier. The team needs a fine tuned model that classifies inbound customer interactions across roughly 80 categories (rebooking, refund, lost baggage, status query, dietary request, special assistance, frequent flyer issue, codeshare issue, and so on). Full fine tuning of a 70B model would require multiple GPUs, days of training time, and produce a 70B parameter copy of the model that needs its own deployment infrastructure. The cost is real and the operational overhead is significant.

LoRA changes the math. The team can fine tune a small adapter (maybe 0.5 percent of the model parameters) on a single GPU in a few hours. The base model stays the same. The adapter modifies behaviour at inference time without changing the underlying weights. Serving the fine tuned model means loading the base model into GPU memory and applying the adapter, which adds essentially zero latency.

The bigger win is that LoRA enables multiple fine tuned variants on the same base model. Qantas could have one base 70B model in production, with separate LoRA adapters for customer service classification, marketing copy generation, internal knowledge search, and a few other use cases. Each adapter is small, can be swapped in per request, and runs on the same underlying infrastructure. The GPU footprint is one base model, not five separate ones.

The cost saving at airline scale would be substantial. A naive architecture with five separate full fine tuned models might cost AUD 400K per year in inference infrastructure. The LoRA architecture might cost AUD 80K for the same capability. The quality difference, on the specific narrow tasks the adapters were trained for, is typically within a percentage point of full fine tuning.

The interesting operational question is who manages the adapters. They are not the same as model deployments. They have lifecycle considerations (when does a Q3 trained adapter get retired, what regression testing applies to a new adapter version). The MLOps discipline for adapter management is newer and less standardised than for full model deployments. Teams that grow into this without thinking about governance end up with adapter sprawl.

For AI delivery, the lesson is that LoRA is what makes self hosted fine tuning practical for enterprise scale. The technical primitive is mature, the economics work, and the operational patterns are emerging. The mature delivery posture is to assume LoRA as the default for any open weight fine tuning, and to design for adapter portfolio management from day one rather than discovering it later.
items.body_zh:
**定义**

LoRA (Low Rank Adaptation) 是参数高效 fine tuning 最常见的形式。LoRA 不是在训练期间更新大型模型的所有权重,而是冻结原始权重并训练一小组额外的权重,通常是总数的 0.1 到 1%。结果表现得像 fine tuned 模型,但训练和服务都便宜得多。

**为何在交付中重要**

大型模型的完整 fine tuning 昂贵、缓慢,并产生你必须托管的模型的单独完整副本。LoRA 改变经济学。你可以在数小时内在单个 GPU 上 fine tune 大型 open weight 模型,而不是在集群上数周。你还可以在同一基础模型之上为不同客户堆叠多个 LoRA 适应,大幅降低服务成本。这是使自托管 fine tuning 对大多数团队实际可行的技术。

**运作原理**

| 方法 | 训练什么 | 训练成本 | 服务成本 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 完整 fine tuning | 所有模型权重 | 非常高 (集群,数天到数周) | 完整大小模型 |
| LoRA | 小适配器矩阵 (权重的 0.1 到 1%) | 低 (单 GPU,数小时) | 基础模型加微小适配器 |
| QLoRA | 在量化 (压缩) 模型上的 LoRA | 最低 (消费 GPU 可能) | 更低的内存 |
| 前缀调整 | 前置到输入的训练虚拟 tokens | 低 | 向上下文添加 tokens |

视觉上,完整 fine tuning 像重写模型。LoRA 像附加一个小的"个性模块",在推理时修改模型的行为,而不改变底层权重。

服务好处是巨大的: 你可以每请求交换 LoRA 适配器,所以一个基础模型可以服务数十个 fine tuned 变体,而无需将单独的模型加载到内存中。

**PM 决策点**

- 项目是在做适用 LoRA 的 open weight fine tuning,还是提供商处理的 closed API fine tuning?
- 系统是否将服务多个 fine tuned 变体,在那里 LoRA 的适配器交换闪耀?
- 团队是否测试了 LoRA 与完整 fine tuning,质量差距通常可以忽略?

**注意事项**

- LoRA 质量对风格和语气优秀,对教真正新知识稍弱
- LoRA 适配器是模型特定的,切换基础模型意味着重做工作
- Closed API fine tuning 经常在引擎盖下使用 LoRA 而不告诉你,这没问题

**要点总结: LoRA 使 fine tuning 实际可行。除非有清晰的理由完全参数化,否则将其作为自托管 fine tuning 的默认。**

**Qantas 案例**

如果 Qantas 要在生产规模上操作 fine tuned 模型,LoRA 几乎肯定是正确的方法。经济学差异是 fine tuning 是好奇心和实际生产模式之间的差异。

考虑之前的假设 Qantas 客户服务分类用例。团队需要一个 fine tuned 模型,跨大约 80 个类别 (重新预订、退款、行李丢失、状态查询、饮食请求、特殊援助、frequent flyer 问题、代码共享问题等等) 分类入站客户互动。70B 模型的完整 fine tuning 需要多个 GPU、数天的训练时间,并产生模型的 70B 参数副本,需要自己的部署基础设施。成本是真实的,运营开销显著。

LoRA 改变数学。团队可以在数小时内在单个 GPU 上 fine tune 一个小适配器 (可能是模型参数的 0.5%)。基础模型保持不变。适配器在推理时修改行为,而不改变底层权重。服务 fine tuned 模型意味着将基础模型加载到 GPU 内存并应用适配器,这增加基本上零的延迟。

更大的胜利是 LoRA 在同一基础模型上启用多个 fine tuned 变体。Qantas 可以在生产中有一个基础 70B 模型,带客户服务分类、营销文案生成、内部知识搜索,以及其他几个用例的单独 LoRA 适配器。每个适配器很小,可以每请求交换,并在相同的底层基础设施上运行。GPU 占用空间是一个基础模型,而不是五个单独的。

在航空规模上的成本节省将是可观的。带五个单独完整 fine tuned 模型的天真架构可能在推理基础设施上每年花费 40 万澳元。LoRA 架构对相同能力可能每年花费 8 万澳元。在适配器训练用于的特定窄任务上,质量差异通常在完整 fine tuning 的一个百分点内。

有趣的运营问题是谁管理适配器。它们与模型部署不同。它们有生命周期考虑 (Q3 训练的适配器何时退休,新适配器版本应用什么回归测试)。适配器管理的 MLOps 纪律比完整模型部署更新且较少标准化。在不考虑治理的情况下增长到这一点的团队最终得到适配器蔓延。

对 AI 交付来说,启示是 LoRA 使企业规模的自托管 fine tuning 实际可行。技术原语是成熟的,经济学有效,运营模式正在出现。成熟的交付姿态是假设 LoRA 作为任何 open weight fine tuning 的默认,并从第一天起为适配器组合管理设计,而不是稍后发现它。

items.title_en: Distillation: teaching a small model to mimic a big one
items.title_zh: 蒸馏: 教小模型模仿大模型
items.body_en:
**Definition**

Distillation is the practice of training a smaller model to imitate the outputs of a larger, more capable model. The large model generates examples, the small model learns from those examples. The result is a small model that performs much better than its size would suggest, on the specific tasks it was distilled for.

**Why it matters in delivery**

Frontier models are expensive and slow. For high volume production workloads, this becomes a real cost and latency problem. Distillation lets you capture most of the frontier model's quality in a small fast cheap model, often at one tenth or one twentieth the inference cost. For the right use case, distillation is the highest leverage cost optimisation in the AI stack.

**How it works**

The basic flow:

1. Define the task (e.g. classifying support tickets, summarising documents)
2. Run a large model (the teacher) on thousands to tens of thousands of real or synthetic examples
3. Capture the teacher's inputs and outputs as training data
4. Fine tune a small model (the student) on that data using SFT
5. Evaluate the student against the teacher on a held out test set
6. If the student is close enough, deploy it for the task

| Layer | Teacher | Student |
|---|---|---|
| Model size | Large (200B+ params, frontier API) | Small (3B to 70B, often open weight) |
| Cost per call | High | 5x to 50x cheaper |
| Latency | Slow | Often 3x to 10x faster |
| Capability | Broad, handles novel queries | Narrow, only good at distilled tasks |

Distillation works because the small model does not need to be generally intelligent, it just needs to mimic the teacher on the specific task. The teacher's "thinking" is implicitly transferred through the examples.

**PM decision points**

- Is the workload high enough volume to justify the engineering effort of distillation?
- Is the task narrow and well defined, distillation does not work well on open ended tasks?
- Has the team evaluated the student rigorously, distillation can hide subtle quality drops?

**Watch outs**

- Distillation locks in the teacher's mistakes, if the teacher hallucinates, the student learns to hallucinate too
- Some model licences restrict using outputs to train other models, check terms (e.g. OpenAI, some China models)
- The student will not generalise to tasks outside the distilled scope, it is a specialist not a generalist

**Takeaway: distillation is the cost optimisation move once a task is stable and high volume. It trades flexibility for economics.**

**Qantas story**

Distillation is one of the highest leverage cost optimisations available to Qantas for high volume narrow AI tasks. The pattern fits a specific shape of workload, and recognising the shape is the skill.

Consider an example workload: tagging inbound customer service interactions with intent categories, sentiment, and urgency. Volume might run to two million interactions per month. Quality requirements are real but bounded: the intent classification needs to be 95 percent accurate against a human labelled gold standard, sentiment classification needs to be 90 percent accurate, urgency classification needs to be 92 percent accurate. The frontier model can do this work easily but at significant cost.

The distillation approach works as follows. First, run the frontier model (say Claude Sonnet) on a stratified sample of fifty thousand real interactions, capturing inputs and outputs. This costs maybe AUD 800 in one off model spend. Second, fine tune a smaller model (say a Llama 8B variant) on the captured pairs using SFT plus LoRA. Training time on a single GPU is a few hours. Third, evaluate the student model on a held out test set against the teacher. If the student is within an acceptable quality range, deploy it.

The cost economics shift dramatically. The frontier model at full volume might cost AUD 90K per month. The distilled student model self hosted on Bedrock with provisioned throughput might cost AUD 6K per month. The savings pay back the distillation engineering effort within the first month.

The interesting edge cases are worth understanding. Distillation works well when the task is narrow and the teacher's behaviour is consistent. It works poorly when the task is open ended or when the teacher's outputs vary by context in ways the student cannot capture. Distillation also locks in the teacher's mistakes, so if the teacher has a known weakness (say, misclassifying a specific edge case 5 percent of the time), the student will inherit it. Validation against ground truth, not just teacher outputs, is important.

The licensing considerations matter too. Some model providers restrict using their outputs to train competing models. Most closed APIs from major providers allow distillation for the customer's own use but restrict commercial training. The legal team needs to review terms before launching a distillation pipeline at scale.

For AI delivery, the lesson is that distillation is the cost lever that turns a successful pilot into a sustainable production system. When a pilot proves a frontier model can do the work well, the next question is "can we capture that capability in a smaller model at lower cost." If the task is narrow and high volume, the answer is usually yes. Clients are often unaware of this lever, and walking them through it during scoping plants the right seed for future cost optimisation.
items.body_zh:
**定义**

蒸馏是训练较小模型模仿较大、更有能力模型的输出的实践。大模型生成示例,小模型从这些示例学习。结果是一个表现得比其大小所暗示的好得多的小模型,在它被蒸馏用于的特定任务上。

**为何在交付中重要**

前沿模型昂贵且缓慢。对于高量生产工作负载,这变成真正的成本和延迟问题。蒸馏让你在小型快速便宜的模型中捕捉前沿模型的大部分质量,通常以推理成本的十分之一或二十分之一。对于正确的用例,蒸馏是 AI 栈中最高杠杆的成本优化。

**运作原理**

基本流程:

1. 定义任务 (例如,分类支持工单、总结文档)
2. 在数千到数万个真实或合成示例上运行大模型 (老师)
3. 捕捉老师的输入和输出作为训练数据
4. 在该数据上使用 SFT fine tune 小模型 (学生)
5. 在保留的测试集上根据老师评估学生
6. 如果学生足够接近,为该任务部署它

| 层级 | 老师 | 学生 |
|---|---|---|
| 模型大小 | 大型 (200B+ 参数,前沿 API) | 小型 (3B 到 70B,通常 open weight) |
| 每调用成本 | 高 | 便宜 5 倍到 50 倍 |
| 延迟 | 慢 | 通常快 3 倍到 10 倍 |
| 能力 | 广泛,处理新查询 | 窄,仅在蒸馏任务上好 |

蒸馏工作因为小模型不需要广泛智能,它只需要在特定任务上模仿老师。老师的"思考"通过示例隐式地转移。

**PM 决策点**

- 工作负载是否足够高量,以证明蒸馏的工程努力合理?
- 任务是否窄且定义良好,蒸馏在开放式任务上效果不佳?
- 团队是否严格评估了学生,蒸馏可以掩盖微妙的质量下降?

**注意事项**

- 蒸馏锁定老师的错误,如果老师幻觉,学生学会幻觉
- 一些模型许可证限制使用输出训练其他模型,检查条款 (例如,OpenAI、一些中国模型)
- 学生不会泛化到蒸馏范围之外的任务,它是专家而不是通才

**要点总结: 一旦任务稳定且高量,蒸馏是成本优化举措。它用灵活性换取经济学。**

**Qantas 案例**

蒸馏是 Qantas 高量窄 AI 任务可用的最高杠杆成本优化之一。模式适合特定形状的工作负载,识别形状是技能。

考虑一个示例工作负载: 用意图类别、情绪和紧急程度标记入站客户服务互动。量可能每月达到两百万次互动。质量要求是真实但有界的: 意图分类需要相对人类标注的金标准达到 95% 准确,情绪分类需要 90% 准确,紧急程度分类需要 92% 准确。前沿模型可以轻松完成这项工作,但成本可观。

蒸馏方法如下工作。首先,在五万个真实互动的分层样本上运行前沿模型 (比如 Claude Sonnet),捕捉输入和输出。这一次性模型支出可能花费 800 澳元。第二,使用 SFT 加 LoRA 在捕捉的对上 fine tune 较小的模型 (比如 Llama 8B 变体)。在单个 GPU 上的训练时间是几小时。第三,在保留的测试集上根据老师评估学生模型。如果学生在可接受的质量范围内,部署它。

成本经济学戏剧性地转变。完整量的前沿模型可能每月花费 9 万澳元。在 Bedrock 上自托管带预配吞吐量的蒸馏学生模型可能每月花费 6,000 澳元。节省在第一个月内偿还蒸馏工程努力。

值得了解的有趣边缘情况。蒸馏在任务窄且老师行为一致时效果良好。在任务开放式或当老师的输出以学生无法捕捉的方式因上下文而变化时效果不佳。蒸馏还锁定老师的错误,所以如果老师有已知的弱点 (比如,5% 的时间误分类特定边缘情况),学生将继承它。验证针对真值,而不仅仅是老师输出,很重要。

许可考虑也重要。一些模型提供商限制使用其输出训练竞争模型。主要提供商的大多数 closed API 允许客户自己使用的蒸馏,但限制商业训练。法律团队需要在大规模启动蒸馏 pipeline 之前审查条款。

对 AI 交付来说,启示是蒸馏是将成功试点变成可持续生产系统的成本杠杆。当试点证明前沿模型可以很好地完成工作时,下一个问题是"我们能否在较小模型中以较低成本捕捉该能力"。如果任务窄且高量,答案通常是肯定的。客户经常不知道这个杠杆,在需求确定期间引导他们通过它为未来的成本优化播下正确的种子。

items.title_en: The trap: clients ask for fine tuning when they really need better prompts or data
items.title_zh: 陷阱: 客户要求 fine tuning,而他们真正需要更好的 prompts 或数据
items.body_en:
**Definition**

The "fine tuning trap" is the pattern where a client asks for fine tuning because it sounds like the serious, sophisticated solution, when the actual problem is poor prompting, missing context, bad data, or unclear requirements. Fine tuning becomes a way to look productive without solving the real problem.

**Why it matters in delivery**

This is one of the most common scoping mistakes in enterprise AI. PMs who recognise it can redirect the client toward what will actually work, save the budget, ship faster, and avoid the political damage of a fine tuning project that delivers nothing. The trap is everywhere because fine tuning sounds like real engineering and prompting sounds trivial.

**How it works**

| Client says | Real problem | Right fix |
|---|---|---|
| "We need to train it on our data" | Model lacks access to client data | RAG, not fine tuning |
| "It does not sound like us" | System prompt lacks tone guidance and examples | Better system prompt with few shot |
| "It hallucinates on our terminology" | No grounding in client vocabulary | RAG over glossary, prompt with key terms |
| "It is inconsistent" | Temperature too high, prompt too vague | Lower temperature, tighten prompt |
| "It is not as good as ChatGPT" | Wrong model tier or prompt for the task | Test stronger model, improve prompt |
| "We have lots of historical data" | Solution looking for a problem | Define the use case first, then decide |

The trap usually shows up after a disappointing prototype. Someone says "we should fine tune." Heads nod. Months get burned.

**PM decision points**

- Has the team built a strong system prompt and tested it rigorously before considering fine tuning?
- Is the problem actually a knowledge gap (RAG fixes it) or a behaviour gap (better prompt usually fixes it)?
- What is the specific gap fine tuning would close that nothing else can?

**Watch outs**

- Clients sometimes want fine tuning for the optics, "we trained our own model" is a status line, push back politely
- A weak prompt makes the model look bad and creates demand for fine tuning to fix something prompting would have solved
- If you do fine tune, build the eval first, otherwise you cannot prove it worked

**Takeaway: fine tuning is the last resort, not the first. Most "we need fine tuning" requests are really "we need a better prompt or better data."**

**Qantas story**

The fine tuning trap is alive and well in large enterprises, and Qantas would be no exception. The pattern is so consistent it is almost predictable. A team is excited about AI, has access to "lots of data," and proposes fine tuning as the obvious sophisticated solution. The right delivery response is to slow down and ask a series of careful questions.

Consider a hypothetical Qantas team running customer experience research. They have years of customer feedback comments, NPS verbatims, and complaint letters. They propose fine tuning a model on this corpus "so it understands Qantas customers." The proposal is well intentioned and would absorb six months of engineering effort.

The diagnostic questions surface the real problem. What is the model going to do that prompting cannot? The team's actual need is to summarise themes across thousands of customer comments and identify emerging concerns. That is a prompting and clustering problem, not a fine tuning problem. A strong system prompt with five example comment summaries, plus a clustering step using embeddings, solves the actual problem in two weeks.

Another team wants to fine tune for "Qantas tone" in customer service responses. The diagnostic question is whether they have tried strong few shot prompting first. The honest answer is usually no. Five well chosen example responses in the system prompt typically captures 90 percent of the tone gap. The remaining 10 percent is real but rarely worth a fine tuning project.

The trap is hardest to navigate when the desire for fine tuning is partly strategic rather than technical. Leaders sometimes want to say "we have our own AI model" as a competitive signal. The delivery practitioner cannot just say no; they need to acknowledge the strategic intent and offer a path that delivers it. That might mean fine tuning a model on a narrow well defined task where the technical case is strong, and using that as the story of "Qantas's custom AI capability" while the broader portfolio uses simpler approaches.

The other version of the trap is data driven. A team has built a labelled dataset and feels obligated to "use it for fine tuning" rather than letting it sit. The right response is that good evaluation data is often more valuable as eval data than as training data. Use the dataset to measure prompt quality, not to train a model that might not be needed.

For AI delivery, the broader lesson is that "we need fine tuning" is almost always a hypothesis to be tested, not a conclusion to be acted on. The discipline is to build a strong baseline with prompting and retrieval, measure the gap rigorously, and only then consider fine tuning for the specific residual problem. Most of the time, the baseline is enough. The clients who appreciate this approach are the ones who have been burned previously by fine tuning projects that delivered less than promised. They learn to value a practitioner who can explain calmly why fine tuning is unnecessary for their specific case.
items.body_zh:
**定义**

"fine tuning 陷阱"是客户要求 fine tuning 的模式,因为它听起来是认真的、复杂的解决方案,而实际问题是糟糕的 prompting、缺失的上下文、糟糕的数据或不清晰的需求。Fine tuning 成为看起来高产而不实际解决问题的方式。

**为何在交付中重要**

这是企业 AI 中最常见的需求确定错误之一。识别它的 PM 可以将客户重新引导到实际有效的方向,节省预算,更快发布,并避免交付什么都没有的 fine tuning 项目的政治损害。陷阱无处不在,因为 fine tuning 听起来像真正的工程,而 prompting 听起来微不足道。

**运作原理**

| 客户说 | 真正的问题 | 正确的修复 |
|---|---|---|
| "我们需要用我们的数据训练它" | 模型缺乏对客户数据的访问 | RAG,不是 fine tuning |
| "它听起来不像我们" | system prompt 缺乏语气指导和示例 | 带 few shot 的更好 system prompt |
| "它在我们的术语上幻觉" | 客户词汇上没有接地 | 在词汇表上的 RAG,带关键术语的 prompt |
| "它不一致" | temperature 太高,prompt 太模糊 | 降低 temperature,收紧 prompt |
| "它不如 ChatGPT 好" | 错误的模型层级或任务的 prompt | 测试更强的模型,改进 prompt |
| "我们有很多历史数据" | 寻找问题的解决方案 | 先定义用例,然后决定 |

陷阱通常在令人失望的原型之后出现。有人说"我们应该 fine tune"。头点了。数月被烧毁。

**PM 决策点**

- 在考虑 fine tuning 之前,团队是否构建了强 system prompt 并严格测试它?
- 问题实际上是知识差距 (RAG 修复它) 还是行为差距 (更好的 prompt 通常修复它)?
- fine tuning 将关闭什么具体差距,没有其他东西能?

**注意事项**

- 客户有时为光学要求 fine tuning,"我们训练了自己的模型"是状态线,礼貌地反驳
- 弱 prompt 使模型看起来糟糕,并创造对 fine tuning 修复 prompting 本来会解决的东西的需求
- 如果你 fine tune,首先构建 eval,否则你无法证明它有效

**要点总结: Fine tuning 是最后手段,而不是第一个。大多数"我们需要 fine tuning"请求实际上是"我们需要更好的 prompt 或更好的数据"。**

**Qantas 案例**

fine tuning 陷阱在大型企业中存活并蓬勃发展,Qantas 不会例外。模式是如此一致,几乎可以预测。团队对 AI 兴奋,可以访问"大量数据",并提议 fine tuning 作为明显复杂的解决方案。正确的交付响应是放慢并问一系列仔细的问题。

考虑一个假设的 Qantas 团队运行客户体验研究。他们有多年的客户反馈评论、NPS 直接反馈,以及投诉信。他们提议在这个语料库上 fine tune 模型"使它了解 Qantas 客户"。提议是善意的,会吸收六个月的工程努力。

诊断问题浮现真正的问题。模型将做 prompting 不能做的什么?团队的实际需求是跨数千客户评论总结主题并识别新兴关注。那是一个 prompting 和聚类问题,而不是 fine tuning 问题。带五个示例评论摘要的强 system prompt,加上使用 embeddings 的聚类步骤,在两周内解决实际问题。

另一个团队想为客户服务响应中的"Qantas 语气"fine tune。诊断问题是他们是否先尝试了强 few shot prompting。诚实的答案通常是不。在 system prompt 中精心选择的五个示例响应通常捕捉 90% 的语气差距。剩下的 10% 是真实的,但很少值得 fine tuning 项目。

陷阱最难导航的是当对 fine tuning 的渴望部分是战略性而不是技术性的时。领导有时希望说"我们有自己的 AI 模型"作为竞争信号。交付从业者不能只是说不; 他们需要承认战略意图并提供交付它的路径。这可能意味着在技术案例强的窄定义任务上 fine tune 模型,并将其用作"Qantas 自定义 AI 能力"的故事,而更广泛的组合使用更简单的方法。

陷阱的另一个版本是数据驱动的。团队已经构建了一个标注数据集,感觉有义务"将其用于 fine tuning",而不是让它闲置。正确的响应是好的评估数据通常作为 eval 数据比作为训练数据更有价值。使用数据集衡量 prompt 质量,而不是训练一个可能不需要的模型。

对 AI 交付来说,更广泛的教训是"我们需要 fine tuning"几乎总是要测试的假设,而不是要采取行动的结论。纪律是用 prompting 和检索构建强基线,严格衡量差距,然后只考虑 fine tuning 解决特定残余问题。大多数时候,基线就足够。欣赏这种方法的客户是那些之前被交付不如承诺多的 fine tuning 项目烧伤的客户。他们学会重视一个能够冷静解释为何 fine tuning 对他们的具体情况不必要的从业者。
